PERSONAL
September 22, 1937
Mr. Harold M. Bixby
Vice President for China
Pan American Airways Co.
Manila, Phillipine Islands
Dear Harold:
I have read
with mich interest your personal let-
ter of September 6th and "apologia". You were certainly not alone in
misjudging the course of developments in China over the last six weeks.
Certainly, I was not in a position to make any better forecast from this
distance,
although from what I heard from you and Bond and others who
have been in Chine and comparing it with the feeling I encountered
throughout New York, particularly at the Council on Foreign Relations,
it looks to me as though the people farthest from the scene saw the most
clearly. This is probably just another example of the old difficulty of
not seeing the woods for the trees. Even so, and without claiming any
superiority of judgment, I am going to stick my neck out in a friendly
way to criticize your analysis of the situation with which I do not agree,
although frankly willing to admit that your opinion is as good or possibly
better than mine.
The question is academic, of course, in any case as we
are faced with realities rather than theories.
In your letter of September 6th you again bring up
the old Jack Dempsey simile which you used both three years ago and one
year ago, which makes me inclined to believe that your thinking has gotten
into somewhat of a groove.
Now this Dempsey simile, while very graphic,
does not in my opinion meet the facts of the case.
to somebody of my name coming out from under the desk at the certain risk
of his life. You overlook the fact that when China came out from under
the desk it came out with a brass knuckle on each hand. If, in fact, the
Chinese resistance had been one of final desperation in circumstances simi-
lar to the Dempsey-Morgan controversey, China would not have come out so
well prepared. It must have been in deliberate anticipation of exactly
what has taken place that China expended so much on munitions, including
the aircraft of our friend Bill Pawley, during the last two years; that the
aviation school was operated at Hanchow; and that, if reports are true, a
goodly number of expert German general staff officers are now available to
advise the Chinese high command. It is my humble opinion that beginning
at least two years ago the Generalissimo was prepared to come to a complete
showdown with Japan,
the minute Japan made the next serious agressive
move, such as the Japanese activities around Peking during the first fort-
night in July proved to be.

Undoubtedly the Generalissimo hoped for the maximum of time
past two years he had any expectation of avoiding it by putting up any fake
show and final agreement which would involve any material expansion of the
Japanese sphere of influence in China. In other words I do not think, as
you say, that the Chinese patience became exhausted, but rather that the
Japanese, judging the situation correctly, forced the issue when they did
instead of giving the General any more time to prepare.

for a showdown in 1916 or later.
There is considerable talk here and in the papers to the
effect that the Chinese Government was dragged into this war through pres-
sure of public opinion and inability to restrain the army leaders and the
masses of the people any longer. This theory does not fibe with the fact
of the very complete and ample preparation which was made for this eventu-
have been controlled by the Government if that had been their policy. It
seems more likely that in Japan the
people were dragged in by the army lead-
ers and this may have important repercussions later.
I never could see why it was that there was such wide-spread
opinion among the "China hands" that the next incident would not seriously
involve Shanghai. There were two controlling reasons, to my mind, why the
Japanese had to attack at Shanghai. One was the necessity of their protect-
ing their great number of nationals there from mob violence, and the second
was the important economic consequence to China of paralizing and control-
ling its most important commercial city. It was equally certain that the
Chinese would resist any military activity around Shanghai although every-
body, including the Japanese, miscalculated the vigor of the Chinese resist-
ance around that point.
In any case, however, it seemed to me, and I re-
member so telling Bond here in July, that far from being & safe haven, I
thought the International Settlement might become perhaps the most dangerous
place to be in China. It must be only a question of time before antipathy
towards Japan will turn into antipathy towards all foreigners--if external
aid is not forthcoming.
I am not going to be foolish enough to try to predict the
future course of events other.
than to say that if my theories
as above set
forth are correct, it is a certainty that the Chinese resistance will be
vigorous and long
drawn out. Much must depend on the extent of the military
supplies which they have been able to accumulate during the last two or three
years, and their ability to obtain new supplies in spite of the coastal block-
ade by Japan. Only time will show the answer to these questions and it seems
to me that gasoline supplies will be a vital factor since, unless I am mistaken,
there is no gasoline production in China, and it would be very difficult at
present to bring this in except through channels which the Japanese will al-
most certainly be successful in blockading. However, experience has shown

that nations manage to get small arm ammnition somehow
or other in spite
of the most rigorous restrictions, and with this type of supplies alone the
Chinese should be able to keep up a devastating guerilla warfare for a
very long period. After all, they have only one chance of winning, or
on a daris theme ree,
shall we say saving themselves, in this war and that is to bleed Japan eco-
nomically and financially white by forcing her to keep a very large army
mobile in the field for a long period. If they do, something is going to
crack badly in Japan, I think,
before anything cracks in China. It is for
this reason that I cannot believe in any return to peaceful conditions in
the future as far ahead as I can see--which means, of course, that in my
opinion there is not the slightest chance of our resuming operations or
participating in operations in China even if we were disposed to make the
necessary further investment.
I have felt all along that the possibility of our operating
a purely commercial service was illusory, not so much because of the fail-

properties.sfomuseum:description: Typewritten letter from S. [Stokely] W. Morgan to Harold M. Bixby, dated September 22, 1937, marked “Personal”; reply to Mr. Bixby’s letter dated September 6 (2019.121.1028); includes critique of Bixby’s analysis of China’s response to the Japanese invasion; mentions Bill [William] Pawley, the Generalissimo [Chiang Kai-shek], [William L.] Bond.
